In \(\text{CH}_4\) the carbon atom has **four bond pairs and no lone pair**, and by the VSEPR model these four electron pairs take up positions in space that minimise their mutual repulsion, i.e. that keep them as far apart as possible.

- In a **square planar** arrangement all four C–H bonds lie in one plane and the H–C–H angle is \(90^\circ\).
- In a **tetrahedral** arrangement the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron and the H–C–H angle is \(109.5^\circ\).

Since \(109.5^\circ > 90^\circ\), the bond pairs are further apart in the tetrahedral arrangement, the bond pair–bond pair repulsion is smaller and the energy of the molecule is lower. The tetrahedral form is therefore the more stable one.

The same conclusion follows from hybridisation: carbon's one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals mix to give four equivalent \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals which are themselves directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron at \(109.5^\circ\), and this is confirmed by the experimentally observed H–C–H angle of \(109.5^\circ\).

Hence \(\text{CH}_4\) is tetrahedral and not square planar.

In \(\text{BeH}_2\) beryllium has only two valence electrons, both of which are used in bonding, so the central atom carries **two bond pairs and no lone pair**. The two pairs get as far apart as possible, which makes the molecule **linear** with H–Be–H \(= 180^\circ\).

Each Be–H bond is indeed polar, because hydrogen and beryllium differ in electronegativity, so each bond has a bond dipole of the same magnitude.

However, for a polyatomic molecule the dipole moment is the **vector sum** of the individual bond dipoles, not their arithmetic sum. In a linear molecule the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions along the same line, so they cancel completely:

\(\mu_{\text{net}} = \mu_{\text{Be-H}} - \mu_{\text{Be-H}} = 0\)

The molecule therefore has a zero net dipole moment although its bonds are polar. This is the same reason that \(\text{BeF}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\), both linear, have zero dipole moments while their bonds are polar.

**\(\text{NH}_3\) has the higher dipole moment.** Measured values: \(\text{NH}_3 = 4.90 \times 10^{-30}\,\text{C m}\ (1.47\,\text{D})\) against \(\text{NF}_3 = 0.8 \times 10^{-30}\,\text{C m}\ (0.23\,\text{D})\).

This is the reverse of what the electronegativities alone would suggest, since fluorine is much more electronegative than hydrogen and so the N–F bonds are the more polar of the two.

The explanation lies in the **direction** of the bond dipoles relative to the lone pair. Both molecules are pyramidal with a lone pair on nitrogen, and that lone pair contributes its own orbital dipole.

- In \(\text{NH}_3\), nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so each N–H bond dipole points towards nitrogen. The resultant of the three N–H bond moments therefore points in the **same** direction as the orbital dipole of the lone pair, and the two ADD.
- In \(\text{NF}_3\), fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, so each N–F bond dipole points away from nitrogen, towards fluorine. The resultant of the three N–F bond moments now points **opposite** to the orbital dipole of the lone pair, and the two partly CANCEL.

The orbital dipole due to the lone pair thus reinforces the bond moments in ammonia and opposes them in nitrogen trifluoride, which is why \(\text{NH}_3\) has the larger dipole moment despite having the less polar bonds.

**Hybridisation** is the process of intermixing of the orbitals of slightly different energies so as to redistribute their energies, resulting in the formation of a new set of orbitals of equivalent energies and shape. The new orbitals are called **hybrid orbitals**, and it is these, not the pure atomic orbitals, that are used in bond formation.

Its main features are: the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals hybridised; the hybrid orbitals are all equivalent in energy and shape; they form stronger bonds than the pure atomic orbitals; and they are directed in space so as to keep the electron pairs as far apart as possible — which is why the type of hybridisation fixes the geometry of the molecule.

**\(sp\) hybridisation.** One \(s\) and one \(p\) orbital mix to give **two** \(sp\) hybrid orbitals, each with 50% \(s\)-character and 50% \(p\)-character. Each has a large positive lobe and a very small negative lobe, and the two point in **opposite directions along one axis, at \(180^\circ\)** — a **linear** (diagonal) arrangement. Example: \(\text{BeCl}_2\).

**\(sp^2\) hybridisation.** One \(s\) and two \(p\) orbitals mix to give **three** equivalent \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of an equilateral triangle, **\(120^\circ\) apart in one plane** — a **trigonal planar** arrangement. Example: \(\text{BCl}_3\).

**\(sp^3\) hybridisation.** One \(s\) and three \(p\) orbitals mix to give **four** equivalent \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals, each with 25% \(s\)-character and 75% \(p\)-character, directed towards the four corners of a **tetrahedron at \(109.5^\circ\)** to one another. Example: \(\text{CH}_4\).

**Yes — the hybridisation of aluminium changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\).**

In \(\text{AlCl}_3\) aluminium uses three of its valence orbitals to form three Al–Cl bonds and has no lone pair, so it is **\(sp^2\) hybridised** and the molecule is **trigonal planar** with Cl–Al–Cl \(= 120^\circ\). One unhybridised \(p\) orbital on aluminium is left **empty**, and aluminium is surrounded by only six electrons — an incomplete octet, which is why \(\text{AlCl}_3\) readily accepts an electron pair.

When a chloride ion approaches, it donates one of its lone pairs into that vacant orbital, forming a coordinate bond:

\(\text{AlCl}_3 + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AlCl}_4^-\)

Aluminium now has **four** bond pairs and no lone pair, so one \(s\) and three \(p\) orbitals are used; it becomes **\(sp^3\) hybridised** and the \(\text{AlCl}_4^-\) ion is **tetrahedral** with a bond angle of \(109.5^\circ\). Aluminium has also completed its octet.

Change: \(sp^2\) (trigonal planar) \(\rightarrow\) \(sp^3\) (tetrahedral).

[Note: the chapter names \(\text{AlCl}_3\) only as an example of an incomplete octet and does not state its hybridisation; the \(sp^2\) assignment follows from the same argument the chapter gives for \(\text{BCl}_3\).]

**Boron changes its hybridisation; nitrogen does not.**

**Boron.** In \(\text{BF}_3\) boron forms three B–F bonds and has no lone pair, so it is **\(sp^2\) hybridised** and the molecule is trigonal planar with F–B–F \(= 120^\circ\). One unhybridised \(p\) orbital is empty and boron has only six electrons around it — an incomplete octet. In the adduct \(\text{F}_3\text{B}\!\cdot\!\text{NH}_3\) boron has accepted a lone pair into that vacant orbital, so it now has **four** bond pairs and becomes **\(sp^3\) hybridised**, the geometry about boron changing from trigonal planar to tetrahedral.

**Nitrogen.** In \(\text{NH}_3\) nitrogen has three bond pairs and one lone pair — four electron pairs in all — so it is already **\(sp^3\) hybridised** (pyramidal). In the adduct that lone pair has become a bond pair by donation to boron, but nitrogen still has four electron pairs around it, so it **remains \(sp^3\)**. Only the geometry about nitrogen changes, from trigonal pyramidal to tetrahedral, because the lone pair that was compressing the H–N–H angles is now a bonding pair.

Summary: B goes \(sp^2 \rightarrow sp^3\); N stays \(sp^3\) throughout.

**The double bond in \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\) (ethene).** Each carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised: one \(2s\) and two \(2p\) orbitals mix to give three \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals lying in a plane at \(120^\circ\), leaving **one unhybridised \(2p\) orbital perpendicular to that plane** on each carbon.

Draw the two carbons side by side. One \(sp^2\) orbital of each carbon overlaps **axially** (end-on) with an \(sp^2\) orbital of the other, giving the \(sp^2\!-\!sp^2\) **sigma** bond between them. The remaining two \(sp^2\) orbitals on each carbon overlap axially with the \(1s\) orbitals of two hydrogen atoms, giving four \(sp^2\!-\!s\) sigma bonds. The two unhybridised \(p\) orbitals, one on each carbon, are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the molecular plane; they overlap **sideways** to form a **pi** bond, whose electron cloud appears as two equal charged clouds, one above and one below the plane of the atoms.

So the C=C double bond is **one sigma bond + one pi bond**. The C=C bond length is \(134\,\text{pm}\), the C–H bond length \(108\,\text{pm}\), the H–C–H angle \(117.6^\circ\) and the H–C–C angle \(121^\circ\).

**The triple bond in \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\) (ethyne).** Each carbon atom is \(sp\) hybridised: one \(2s\) and one \(2p\) orbital mix to give two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals pointing in opposite directions, leaving **two unhybridised \(p\) orbitals** \((2p_x\) and \(2p_y)\) on each carbon, mutually perpendicular.

One \(sp\) orbital of each carbon overlaps axially with an \(sp\) orbital of the other to give the C–C **sigma** bond; the other \(sp\) orbital of each carbon overlaps axially with a hydrogen \(1s\) orbital to give a C–H sigma bond. The two pairs of parallel unhybridised \(p\) orbitals then overlap sideways to form **two pi bonds**, whose electron clouds lie in two mutually perpendicular planes about the C–C axis.

So the C≡C triple bond is **one sigma bond + two pi bonds**, and the molecule is linear.

[Note: the question asks for diagrams; the description above states exactly what each diagram must show — the axial overlaps that give the sigma bonds and the sideways overlap of the unhybridised \(p\) orbitals that gives the pi bond(s).]

A single bond is one sigma bond; a double bond is one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond is one sigma and two pi bonds. Every bond to hydrogen is a sigma bond.

**(a) \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\)** — the structure is H–C≡C–H.

- Two C–H bonds \(\rightarrow\) 2 sigma bonds
- The C≡C triple bond \(\rightarrow\) 1 sigma + 2 pi bonds

Total: **3 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds.**

**(b) \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)** — the structure is \(\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2\).

- Four C–H bonds \(\rightarrow\) 4 sigma bonds
- The C=C double bond \(\rightarrow\) 1 sigma + 1 pi bond

Total: **5 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond.**

The hybridisation of a carbon atom follows from the number of sigma bonds it forms: four sigma bonds \(\rightarrow sp^3\); three sigma bonds and one pi bond \(\rightarrow sp^2\); two sigma bonds and two pi bonds \(\rightarrow sp\).

**\(\text{CH}_3\text{--CH}_3\) (ethane)** — each carbon forms four sigma bonds (three to H, one to the other C), so **both carbons are \(sp^3\)**.

**(b) \(\text{CH}_3\text{--CH}=\text{CH}_2\) (propene)** — the methyl carbon forms four sigma bonds and is **\(sp^3\)**; the two doubly bonded carbons each form three sigma bonds and one pi bond and are **\(sp^2\)**.

**(c) \(\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-OH}\) (ethanol)** — every carbon forms four sigma bonds, so **both carbons are \(sp^3\)**.

**(d) \(\text{CH}_3\text{-CHO}\) (ethanal)** — the methyl carbon is **\(sp^3\)**; the carbon of the –CHO group is doubly bonded to oxygen, so it forms three sigma bonds and one pi bond and is **\(sp^2\)**.

**(e) \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\) (acetic acid)** — the methyl carbon is **\(sp^3\)**; the carboxyl carbon is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to the other and to the methyl carbon, so it is **\(sp^2\)**.

[Note: the chapter works out ethane \((sp^3)\), ethene \((sp^2)\) and ethyne \((sp)\) in full; the assignments for the alcohol, the aldehyde and the acid follow from the same count of sigma bonds.]

**Bond pair (shared pair).** A pair of valence electrons that is shared between two atoms and is responsible for the covalent bond between them. It is under the influence of BOTH nuclei, and being shared between two atoms it is comparatively localised in the region between them.

**Lone pair (non-bonding pair).** A pair of valence electrons on an atom that is NOT involved in bonding. It belongs to that atom alone and is under the influence of only one nucleus, so it spreads out and occupies more space than a bond pair.

**Illustration.** In \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) oxygen has six valence electrons. Two of them are used in forming the two O–H bonds, so there are **two bond pairs**; the remaining four stay on oxygen as **two lone pairs**.

In \(\text{NH}_3\) nitrogen has five valence electrons: three are used in the three N–H bonds (**three bond pairs**) and the remaining two stay on nitrogen as **one lone pair**.

The distinction matters because a lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair, which is why the repulsions run lp–lp \(>\) lp–bp \(>\) bp–bp and why bond angles in molecules with lone pairs are smaller than the ideal values.

**Sigma \((\sigma)\) bond**

1. Formed by the **end-to-end (head-on, axial) overlap** of bonding orbitals **along the internuclear axis**.
2. Can be formed by \(s\!-\!s\), \(s\!-\!p\) or \(p\!-\!p\) overlap.
3. The overlapping takes place to a **larger** extent, so the bond is **stronger**.
4. The electron cloud is symmetrical about the internuclear axis.
5. It can exist independently — a single bond is always a sigma bond, and every multiple bond contains exactly one.
6. Free rotation about a sigma bond is possible.

**Pi \((\pi)\) bond**

1. Formed by the **sideways (lateral) overlap** of orbitals whose axes remain **parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis**.
2. Formed only by the overlap of \(p\) (or \(d\)) orbitals; \(s\) orbitals cannot form it.
3. The overlapping takes place to a **smaller** extent, so the bond is **weaker**.
4. The electron cloud consists of two saucer-shaped charged clouds lying above and below the plane of the participating atoms, and is not symmetrical about the internuclear axis.
5. It **never exists on its own** — a pi bond is always formed in addition to a sigma bond, in a double or triple bond.
6. Rotation about a pi bond is not possible without breaking it.

Consider two hydrogen atoms A and B, with nuclei \(N_A\) and \(N_B\) and electrons \(e_A\) and \(e_B\). While the atoms are far apart there is no interaction between them. As they approach, new forces begin to operate.

**Attractive forces arise between**

(i) the nucleus of one atom and its own electron, \(N_A\!-\!e_A\) and \(N_B\!-\!e_B\);
(ii) the nucleus of one atom and the electron of the other, \(N_A\!-\!e_B\) and \(N_B\!-\!e_A\).

**Repulsive forces arise between**

(i) the electrons of the two atoms, \(e_A\!-\!e_B\);
(ii) the nuclei of the two atoms, \(N_A\!-\!N_B\).

Experimentally the magnitude of the new attractive forces is greater than that of the new repulsive forces. The two atoms therefore approach each other and the potential energy of the system falls. Ultimately a stage is reached at which the net force of attraction just balances the force of repulsion and the system acquires **minimum energy**; this minimum in the potential-energy curve is the most stable state, and at this point the two atoms are bonded, with a bond length of \(74\,\text{pm}\). Any attempt to push the nuclei still closer causes a sudden rise in energy and destabilises the molecule.

In orbital terms, at this separation the two singly occupied \(1s\) orbitals, holding electrons of **opposite spin**, partially interpenetrate — they overlap along the internuclear axis. This head-on overlap gives a sigma bond, and the greater the overlap the stronger the bond, because the electron density between the nuclei increases and helps to hold them together.

Because energy is released when the bond forms, the molecule is more stable than the two isolated atoms. The energy released is the bond enthalpy, and conversely

\(\text{H}_2(g) + 435.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} \rightarrow \text{H}(g) + \text{H}(g)\)

Atomic orbitals combine linearly to form molecular orbitals only if the following conditions are satisfied.

**1. The combining atomic orbitals must have the same or nearly the same energy.** A \(1s\) orbital of one atom can combine with the \(1s\) orbital of another, but not with a \(2s\) orbital, whose energy is appreciably higher. (This condition is relaxed if the two atoms are very different from each other.)

**2. The combining atomic orbitals must have the same symmetry about the molecular axis.** By convention the \(z\)-axis is taken as the molecular axis. Thus a \(2p_z\) orbital of one atom can combine with the \(2p_z\) orbital of the other, but not with its \(2p_x\) or \(2p_y\) orbitals, because those have a different symmetry about that axis. Orbitals of the same energy will still not combine if their symmetries differ.

**3. The combining atomic orbitals must overlap to the maximum extent.** The greater the extent of overlap, the greater the electron density between the nuclei in the resulting molecular orbital, and hence the more effective the combination.

The electronic configuration of a beryllium atom is \(1s^2\,2s^2\), so a \(\text{Be}_2\) molecule would contain \(2 \times 4 = 8\) electrons. Filling the molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy gives

\(\text{Be}_2 : (\sigma 1s)^2\,(\sigma^* 1s)^2\,(\sigma 2s)^2\,(\sigma^* 2s)^2\)

Number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals, \(N_b = 4\).
Number of electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals, \(N_a = 4\).

Bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a) = \tfrac{1}{2}(4 - 4) = 0\)

A bond order of zero means there is **no net bonding**: every bonding molecular orbital is matched by a filled antibonding molecular orbital, so the stabilisation produced by the bonding electrons is exactly cancelled by the destabilisation produced by the antibonding electrons. The molecule is therefore unstable relative to two separate beryllium atoms, and \(\text{Be}_2\) does not exist.

The same argument applies to \(\text{He}_2\), whose configuration \((\sigma 1s)^2(\sigma^* 1s)^2\) also gives a bond order of zero.

All four species use the molecular-orbital energy order that applies to \(\text{O}_2\):

\(\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < (\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z\)

Starting from \(\text{O}_2\) (16 electrons), the extra or missing electrons go into or come out of the \(\pi^* 2p\) orbitals, so \(N_b = 10\) throughout and only \(N_a\) changes. Bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)\).

**\(\text{O}_2^+\) (15 electrons)** — \(\ldots(\pi 2p_x)^2(\pi 2p_y)^2(\pi^* 2p_x)^1\). \(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 5\), bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10-5) = 2.5\). One unpaired electron \(\rightarrow\) **paramagnetic**.

**\(\text{O}_2\) (16 electrons)** — \(\ldots(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1\). \(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 6\), bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10-6) = 2\). Two unpaired electrons \(\rightarrow\) **paramagnetic**.

**\(\text{O}_2^-\) (superoxide, 17 electrons)** — \(\ldots(\pi^* 2p_x)^2(\pi^* 2p_y)^1\). \(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 7\), bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10-7) = 1.5\). One unpaired electron \(\rightarrow\) **paramagnetic**.

**\(\text{O}_2^{2-}\) (peroxide, 18 electrons)** — \(\ldots(\pi^* 2p_x)^2(\pi^* 2p_y)^2\). \(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 8\), bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10-8) = 1\). All molecular orbitals doubly occupied \(\rightarrow\) **diamagnetic**.

Since stability increases with bond order (bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases), the order of stability is

\(\text{O}_2^+ > \text{O}_2 > \text{O}_2^- > \text{O}_2^{2-}\)

Magnetic behaviour: \(\text{O}_2^+\), \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2^-\) are paramagnetic; \(\text{O}_2^{2-}\) is diamagnetic.

An atomic orbital is described by a wave function \(\psi\), which represents the **amplitude of the electron wave**. Like the amplitude of any wave, it can be positive in one region of space and negative in another.

The plus and minus signs marked on the boundary-surface diagrams of orbitals therefore denote the **sign (phase) of the orbital wave function** in that lobe. **They are not electrical charges** — a lobe marked minus is not negatively charged.

Their significance lies in what happens when two orbitals overlap:

- If the overlapping lobes have the **same sign** and the right orientation in space, the overlap is **positive**: the two electron waves reinforce each other by constructive interference, electron density builds up between the nuclei and a **bonding** molecular orbital of lower energy results.
- If the overlapping lobes have **opposite signs**, the overlap is **negative**: the waves cancel each other by destructive interference, a nodal plane appears between the nuclei and an **antibonding** molecular orbital of higher energy results.
- If the positive and negative contributions exactly cancel, the net overlap is **zero** and no bond is formed at all.

So the signs tell us which combinations of orbitals can actually bond, and they are the reason the symmetry condition must be satisfied before two atomic orbitals may combine.

**Hybridisation in \(\text{PCl}_5\).** Phosphorus \((Z = 15)\) has the ground-state outer configuration \(3s^2\,3p^3\). In the excited state one \(3s\) electron is promoted to a vacant \(3d\) orbital, giving \(3s^1\,3p_x^1\,3p_y^1\,3p_z^1\,3d^1\) — five singly occupied orbitals. These five orbitals (one \(s\), three \(p\) and one \(d\)) then hybridise to give a set of five **\(sp^3d\) hybrid orbitals**, directed towards the five corners of a **trigonal bipyramid**. Each \(sp^3d\) orbital overlaps with a singly occupied \(p\) orbital of a chlorine atom to form five P–Cl sigma bonds.

**The five bonds are not equivalent.** Three P–Cl bonds lie in one plane and make an angle of \(120^\circ\) with one another — these are the **equatorial** bonds. The remaining two P–Cl bonds lie one above and one below that plane, making an angle of \(90^\circ\) with it — these are the **axial** bonds.

**Why the axial bonds are longer.** Each axial bond pair is at \(90^\circ\) to **three** equatorial bond pairs, whereas each equatorial bond pair is at \(90^\circ\) to only **two** bond pairs (the two axial ones), the other two equatorial pairs being a comfortable \(120^\circ\) away. The axial bond pairs therefore suffer more repulsive interaction from the equatorial bond pairs than the equatorial bonds suffer from each other. They are consequently pushed slightly outwards, so the axial bonds are **slightly longer and hence slightly weaker** than the equatorial bonds — which is what makes \(\text{PCl}_5\) so reactive.

**Definition.** A hydrogen bond is the attractive force which binds the hydrogen atom of one molecule with an electronegative atom (F, O or N) of another molecule.

It arises when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom X. The shared electron pair is drawn away from hydrogen towards X, so hydrogen acquires a fractional positive charge \((\delta+)\) and X a fractional negative charge \((\delta-)\). This partially positive hydrogen is then electrostatically attracted to the electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule:

\(\text{H}^{\delta+}\!-\!\text{X}^{\delta-} \cdots \text{H}^{\delta+}\!-\!\text{X}^{\delta-} \cdots \text{H}^{\delta+}\!-\!\text{X}^{\delta-}\)

The hydrogen bond is shown by a dotted line while the covalent bond is shown by a solid line, so the hydrogen atom acts as a bridge, held to one atom by a covalent bond and to the other by a hydrogen bond. It is **weaker than a covalent bond**.

**Compared with van der Waals forces, the hydrogen bond is STRONGER.** Van der Waals forces are the weak, non-directional attractions that exist between all molecules and arise from momentary or permanent dipoles. A hydrogen bond is a much more strongly directional interaction between a highly polarised H–X bond and a specific, small, highly electronegative atom, so it is appreciably the stronger of the two — which is why it has such a marked effect on the structures, boiling points and other properties of compounds such as HF, water and the alcohols.

[Note: this chapter compares the hydrogen bond only with the covalent bond, calling it weaker. It never compares it with van der Waals forces — the phrase "van der Waals" appears in the chapter only in "van der Waals radius", which is a measure of atomic size and not a force. The comparison above is therefore not drawn from this chapter.]

**Bond order** is one half the difference between the number of electrons present in the bonding molecular orbitals and the number present in the antibonding molecular orbitals:

\(\text{Bond order} = \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)\)

A positive bond order \((N_b > N_a)\) means a stable molecule, while a zero or negative bond order means an unstable one. Integral values of 1, 2 and 3 correspond to single, double and triple bonds, and the bond length decreases as the bond order increases.

**\(\text{N}_2\) (14 electrons).** For \(\text{B}_2\), \(\text{C}_2\) and \(\text{N}_2\) the \(\pi 2p\) orbitals lie below \(\sigma 2p_z\):

\(\text{N}_2 : (\sigma 1s)^2(\sigma^* 1s)^2(\sigma 2s)^2(\sigma^* 2s)^2(\pi 2p_x)^2(\pi 2p_y)^2(\sigma 2p_z)^2\)

\(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 4\); bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10 - 4) = \mathbf{3}\)

**\(\text{O}_2\) (16 electrons).** Here \(\sigma 2p_z\) lies below the \(\pi 2p\) orbitals:

\(\text{O}_2 : (\sigma 1s)^2(\sigma^* 1s)^2(\sigma 2s)^2(\sigma^* 2s)^2(\sigma 2p_z)^2(\pi 2p_x)^2(\pi 2p_y)^2(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1\)

\(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 6\); bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = \mathbf{2}\)

**\(\text{O}_2^+\) (15 electrons).** One electron fewer than \(\text{O}_2\), removed from a \(\pi^* 2p\) orbital.

\(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 5\); bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10 - 5) = \mathbf{2.5}\)

**\(\text{O}_2^-\) (17 electrons).** One electron more than \(\text{O}_2\), added to a \(\pi^* 2p\) orbital.

\(N_b = 10,\ N_a = 7\); bond order \(= \tfrac{1}{2}(10 - 7) = \mathbf{1.5}\)

Bond orders: \(\text{N}_2 = 3\), \(\text{O}_2 = 2\), \(\text{O}_2^+ = 2.5\), \(\text{O}_2^- = 1.5\).
